title: Most people read the story of the woman at the well and immediately focus on her shame.
paragraphs: Most people read the story of the woman at the well and immediately focus on her shame.
Five husbands.
Living with a man who was not her husband.

A broken woman.
A sinful woman.
A scandalous woman.
But buried beneath the surface of John chapter 4 is a mystery most people never stop long enough to notice.
Because Jesus was not simply exposing her immorality.
He was unveiling the spiritual history of an entire people.
And once you see it…
the entire conversation changes.
The moment begins in the heat of the day.

Not morning.
Not evening.
Noon.
The hour when nobody wanted to be outside.
Especially a woman carrying shame heavy enough to avoid every other person in town.
John 4:6 says:
“Now Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour.”
The “sixth hour” in Jewish reckoning is noon.
The hottest part of the day.
She came alone because wounded people often learn how to disappear quietly.
And then Jesus speaks.
A Jewish rabbi speaking publicly to a Samaritan woman was already shocking enough.
But this conversation goes deeper than ethnicity, gender, or morality.
It reaches into covenant history.
Into idolatry.
Into spiritual adultery.
Into the ancient fracture between Israel and Samaria.
Jesus says in John 4:16–18:
“Go, call thy husband, and come hither.
The woman answered and said, I have no husband.
Jesus said unto her, Thou hast well said, I have no husband:
For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly.”
Now here is where the mystery begins.
The Greek phrase used for “husband” is:
ἀνήρ (anēr)

This word can mean:
“man”
or
“husband”
depending on context.
But throughout Scripture, marriage language is constantly used symbolically for covenant relationship with God.
Israel was called the wife of Yahweh.
Idolatry was called adultery.
Spiritual rebellion was called harlotry.
This was not metaphor invented later by theologians.
It was embedded deeply in the Hebrew Scriptures.
In Jeremiah 3:20, God says:
“Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me.”
The Hebrew word for husband there is:
בַּעַל (ba‘al)
Which is fascinating because Baal was also the name of a false god worshiped by Israel.

The word itself can mean:
master
owner
husband
Israel literally prostituted covenant intimacy with God by chasing false “baals.”
Now watch this carefully.
The Samaritans were not simply “mixed race Jews.”
Their entire religious history was corrupted by foreign nations planted into the land by Assyria after the fall of the northern kingdom.
2 Kings 17 explains something most believers overlook.
The Assyrians brought multiple foreign peoples into Samaria.
Each group brought their own gods.
Their own worship systems.
Their own idols.
Their own spiritual “husbands.”
2 Kings 17:24 says:
“And the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim…”
Five foreign nations.
Five pagan systems.
Five false gods integrated into Samaritan worship.
Then verses 30–31 list the gods they served.
This is not accidental.
Jesus was speaking to a Samaritan woman who symbolized the spiritual condition of Samaria itself.
A people with five false covenant relationships.
Five spiritual husbands.
And now living with a sixth that was not the true husband either.
The Samaritans claimed to worship Yahweh…
but mixed Him with corrupted worship.
They had religion…
without covenant purity.
Truth mixed with compromise.
And suddenly Jesus’ words become terrifyingly prophetic.
Because He was not merely reading her personal history.
He was unveiling the spiritual history of an entire nation standing right in front of Him.
This is why the woman immediately changes the subject to worship.
“Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet.
Our fathers worshipped in this mountain…”
Why would she suddenly bring up worship?
Because Jesus had just exposed the real issue.
Not merely sexual sin.
False worship.
Broken covenant.
Spiritual confusion.
Then Jesus says something revolutionary.
John 4:23:
“But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth…”
The Greek here matters deeply.
“Truth” is:
ἀλήθεια (alētheia)

Meaning:
reality unveiled
what is unconcealed
ultimate divine truth
Jesus was confronting generations of concealed corruption.
And offering revelation.
Not just condemnation.
This woman becomes a living picture of humanity itself.
Trying to satisfy eternal thirst through broken relationships.
Broken worship.
Broken identities.
Broken substitutes.

Five husbands.
Sixth relationship.
Still thirsty.
And then Jesus says:
“Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst…”
The Greek phrase for “never thirst” is extraordinarily powerful:

οὐ μὴ διψήσει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
(ou mē dipsēsei eis ton aiōna)
Literally:
“Will absolutely never thirst forever.”
Not temporary relief.
Not religious performance.
Not emotional inspiration.
Transformation.
Because Jesus was offering what no husband, no idol, no pleasure, no religion, no system, no addiction, and no worldly identity could ever provide.
Living water.
Notice something devastating.
The woman came to draw water…
but left her waterpot behind.
John 4:28:
“The woman then left her waterpot…”
Why mention the waterpot?
Because encounters with Christ make old survival systems unnecessary.
The thing she came depending on became irrelevant once she met the true source.
And the woman who arrived hiding from people suddenly runs into the city proclaiming Christ openly.
Shame lost its grip the moment truth met grace.
Not watered-down grace.
Not permissive grace.
Transforming grace.
Jesus never affirmed her sin.
But He also did not crush her beneath it.
He exposed her completely…
while still moving toward her with mercy.
That is the Gospel.
Many people today still live exactly like Samaria.
Religious language mixed with idols.
Christian vocabulary mixed with worldly worship.

Trying to merge Jesus with self-worship.
Jesus with lust.
Jesus with pride.
Jesus with political identity.
Jesus with social approval.
Jesus with hidden compromise.
But Christ does not enter into covenant as one more “husband” among many competing idols.
He demands supremacy.
The woman at the well is not merely a story about sexual failure.
It is a revelation about spiritual thirst.
And every human soul eventually learns the same painful truth:
Whatever is not Christ will leave you thirsty again.

Again.
And again.
And again.
Until grace finally breaks the cycle.
The beautiful part is this:
Jesus intentionally traveled through Samaria.
Most Jews avoided it completely.
But John 4:4 says:
“And he must needs go through Samaria.”
“Must” in Greek is:
δεῖ (dei)

Meaning:
it is necessary
divinely required
ordained
This was not random travel.
This was divine appointment.
Jesus went looking for the outcast.

The confused.
The compromised.
The ashamed.
The spiritually thirsty.
And He still does.

Some people reading this have spent years trying to quench soul-thirst with relationships, success, attention, pornography, money, validation, distractions, entertainment, ministry titles, social media, or hidden sin.
Still thirsty.
Because only Christ reaches the deepest well beneath the human heart.
Only Christ speaks truth without destroying the sinner.
Only Christ exposes darkness while offering redemption.
Only Christ can take someone hiding at noon in shame…
and turn them into a witness carrying living water to an entire city.
This is why the Gospel is not behavior modification.
It is resurrection.
And maybe the deepest mystery in the entire story is this:
Jesus already knew everything about her…
and stayed anyway.
That is the kind of Savior He is.
